beats.narration: [intrigued] One equation from a paper about phone-line noise ended up telling Wall Street how much money to bet on every trade.

[curious] In nineteen fifty-six, John Kelly, a physicist at Bell Labs, was working on a puzzle in information theory. [thoughtful] If a gambler's tip is only sometimes right, what fraction of the bankroll should they wager?

[thoughtful] Kelly looked at the wealth as it compounded. Bet a fraction f of the bankroll, win b to one with probability p, lose otherwise. The long-run growth rate per bet is p times log of one plus b f, plus q times log of one minus f. [confident] Take its derivative, set it equal to zero, and one clean answer falls out. f equals b p minus q, divided by b. Bet more than that, you eventually go broke. Bet less, you leave money on the table.

[excited] Ed Thorp learned it from Kelly's paper, took it to Vegas, and beat blackjack by card counting. [confident] Then he brought the same formula to Wall Street, and compounded his money at twenty percent a year for twenty-eight years.
